{ "item": { "id": "1a7f5c3e-cdcd-4181-bd36-a6092afd56cb", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Connecting a data source", "short_description": "Choose the right connector type and authentication method for a new data source.", "body": "

Connecting a data source

This guide covers choosing and configuring a source connector — the first step of any new pipeline.

Choosing a connector type

You haveUse
A relational database you can grant replication access toPostgres
Files landing in object storageAmazon S3
An existing event streamKafka
A third party that can push to a URL you controlWebhook

Authenticating

Each connector type has its own credential shape — see the Connectors endpoint for the full parameter list per type.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Least-privilege credentials|body_html=

Grant the connector only the access it needs — read-only replication for Postgres sources, a scoped IAM role for S3, never a superuser or admin credential.

}}

Verifying the connection

A newly created connector reports health: degraded until its first successful read or write, then flips to healthy. If it goes straight to down, double check credentials before opening a support ticket.

Next steps

With a source connected, follow Transforming events in flight to reshape and filter your data before it reaches its destination.

{ "item": { "id": "dc9f1302-e173-4034-9581-d06efea7d090", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Scheduling & triggers", "short_description": "Run a pipeline on a cron schedule or trigger it directly from incoming events.", "body": "

Scheduling & triggers

A pipeline runs either on a schedule or in response to incoming events. This guide covers both.

Scheduled pipelines

Set a schedule (a cron expression) when creating or updating a pipeline via the Pipelines endpoint. Godzilla runs the pipeline once per schedule tick, processing whatever new data is available from the source since the last run.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=schedule.json|language=json|code={ "schedule": "0 */4 * * *" }}}

Event-triggered pipelines

Omit schedule and the pipeline instead runs continuously, processing events as its source connector emits them — the right choice for sources like Kafka or a Webhook connector where near-real-time matters.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Choosing between them|body_html=

Use a schedule for sources that batch naturally (a nightly file drop to S3). Use event-triggered for anything where minutes matter.

}}

Pausing and resuming

A paused pipeline skips scheduled ticks entirely and buffers nothing for event-triggered sources — resuming picks up new events going forward, not a backlog. To reprocess a time range instead, see the replay flow in Handling errors & retries.

{{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/062cc815-2b65-45b1-b36c-6ea67dfd1a0c}}|prev_label=Handling errors & retries|next_href={{cms:item/522ba05b-8a21-43dd-82ac-ece908ce14b4}}|next_label=Monitoring & alerts}}", "version_token": "79959961-9dce-4f2e-b4ca-b957b12122d0", "created_at": "2026-08-20T14:12:47.158Z", "updated_at": "2026-08-20T15:07:12.086Z", "placement_id": "8ed279da-c9eb-46e0-bd2f-4f15df9f1c76", "folder_id": "c3e0ba4a-a491-4265-9848-556d298e6b6b", "file_name": "scheduling-and-triggers" } }

{ "item": { "id": "522ba05b-8a21-43dd-82ac-ece908ce14b4", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Monitoring & alerts", "short_description": "Watch pipeline health and get notified of failures via webhooks before they become incidents.", "body": "

Monitoring & alerts

Keep an eye on a running pipeline without babysitting it manually.

Connector health

Poll a connector's health field via the Connectors endpoint, or better, subscribe to connector.error so you're notified the moment it degrades.

Subscribing to pipeline lifecycle events

The most reliable way to monitor a pipeline is a webhook subscription on pipeline.failed and connector.error.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=subscribe.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/webhooks \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \ -d '{"url":"https://you.example.com/hooks/godzilla","events":["pipeline.failed","connector.error"]}'}} {{ds:component/alert|variant=success|title=Recommended baseline|body_html=

At minimum, subscribe to pipeline.failed for every production pipeline. It's the single highest-signal event for catching problems before customers do.

}}

Dead-letter queue depth

A growing dead-letter queue is an early warning sign, not just a symptom — see Handling errors & retries for how events end up there and how to drain them.

{{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/dc9f1302-e173-4034-9581-d06efea7d090}}|prev_label=Scheduling & triggers|next_href={{cms:item/60d7d27a-ceda-4034-b98e-8b1181ca5c84}}|next_label=Guides}}", "version_token": "352ca016-eadc-40fe-8762-27fd446580a2", "created_at": "2026-08-20T14:12:53.717Z", "updated_at": "2026-08-20T15:07:12.090Z", "placement_id": "1bf22621-3ed5-4c90-b1d8-47770d74ffd7", "folder_id": "c3e0ba4a-a491-4265-9848-556d298e6b6b", "file_name": "monitoring-and-alerts" } }

{ "item": { "id": "9b29ce8a-e4bb-4aa8-bbd4-afb938586d7f", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Error handling & recovery", "short_description": "How Godzilla retries failed events, when they're dead-lettered, and how to replay them.", "body": "

Error handling & recovery

Every event that fails a transform or a destination write is retried automatically. This guide covers how that works and what to do when retries run out.

Automatic retries

Failed events retry with exponential backoff — 1s, 2s, 4s, up to a per-pipeline configurable ceiling. Most transient failures (a destination hiccup, a rate-limited third party) resolve within the first few attempts.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline-retry-config.json|language=json|code={ \\\"retry_policy\\\": { \\\"max_attempts\\\": 5, \\\"backoff\\\": \\\"exponential\\\", \\\"initial_delay_ms\\\": 1000 } }}}

Dead-lettering

An event that exhausts its retries is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped silently.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=danger|title=Dead-lettered events don't retry themselves|body_html=

Once in the dead-letter queue, an event stays there until you replay it or explicitly discard it — it will not retry again on its own.

}}

Replaying events

Use the Events endpoint's replay action to re-run a specific dead-lettered event once the underlying issue is fixed.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=replay.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/events/evt_8f2c1a90/replay \\\\\\n -H \\\"Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY\\\"}}

Watching for failures

Subscribe to pipeline.failed via Webhooks so you find out about dead-lettered events before a customer does. See also Monitoring & alerts.

{ "item": { "id": "9f11bc60-f95f-44ef-81cf-e822f6692844", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Transforming events in flight", "short_description": "Reshape, filter, and enrich events as they pass through a pipeline.", "body": "

Transforming events in flight

Once events enter your pipeline, you can reshape them, filter out unwanted records, or add enrichment data from external sources — all before they reach their destination.

Reshaping events

Use a transform to extract, rename, or restructure fields from incoming events. Transforms are JavaScript functions that receive an event and return a modified version of it.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=transform.js|language=javascript|code=export default function transform(event) {\n return {\n user_id: event.customer_id,\n name: event.first_name + ' ' + event.last_name,\n email: event.contact_email,\n created_at: new Date(event.signup_timestamp).toISOString()\n };\n}}}

Return null from a transform to drop an event entirely, or throw an error to send it to the dead-letter queue.

Filtering events

Add a filter condition to your transform to block unwanted records at the source. A filter that returns false discards the event; true passes it through.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=filter.js|language=javascript|code=export default function filter(event) {\n // Only pass through events from paying customers\n return event.plan_type !== 'free';\n}}} {{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Filters are fast|body_html=

Filtering in the pipeline is cheaper than transforming and sending to a destination, then filtering downstream. Apply filters early.

}}

Enriching with external data

Building your first pipeline

{{ds:component/docs-toc|items_html=
  • 1. Create a source connector
  • 2. Create a destination connector
  • 3. Create the pipeline
  • Next steps
    • }}

    This guide walks through creating a pipeline end to end: a source connector, a destination connector, and the pipeline that ties them together.

    {{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Before you start|body_html=

    You'll need an API key. See Authentication in Getting Started if you don't have one yet.

    }}

    1. Create a source connector

    We'll pull orders from Postgres. See Connectors for the full catalog of types.

    Bash

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=create-source.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/connectors \\\ -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \ -d '{"type":"postgres","direction":"source","config":{"connection_string":"postgres://..."}}'}}

    Go

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=create_connector.go|language=go|code=package main import ( "context" "log" "os" "github.com/godzilla-io/godzilla-go/client" ) func createSourceConnector(ctx context.Context, c *client.Client) (string, error) { connector, err := c.Connectors.Create(ctx, &client.CreateConnectorRequest{ Type: "postgres", Direction: "source", Config: map[string]interface{}{ "connection_string": "postgres://...", }, }) return connector.ID, err }}}

    2. Create a destination connector

    We'll write to Snowflake.

    Bash

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=create-destination.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/connectors \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \ -d '{"type":"snowflake","direction":"destination","config":{"account":"..."}}'}}

    Go

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=create_connector.go|language=go|code=func createDestinationConnector(ctx context.Context, c *client.Client) (string, error) { connector, err := c.Connectors.Create(ctx, &client.CreateConnectorRequest{ Type: "snowflake", Direction: "destination", Config: map[string]interface{}{ "account": "...", }, }) return connector.ID, err }}}

    3. Create the pipeline

    Full request/response details are in the Pipelines endpoint reference.

    Bash

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=create-pipeline.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/pipelines \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \ -d '{"name":"ingest-orders","source_connector_id":"conn_pg_orders","destination_connector_id":"conn_snowflake_dw"}'}}

    Go

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=create_pipeline.go|language=go|code=package main import ( "context" "log" "os" "github.com/godzilla-io/godzilla-go/client" ) func main() { apiKey := os.Getenv("GODZILLA_API_KEY") c := client.New(apiKey) pipeline, err := c.Pipelines.Create(context.Background(), &client.CreatePipelineRequest{ Name: "ingest-orders", SourceConnectorID: "conn_pg_orders", DestinationConnectorID: "conn_snowflake_dw", }) if err != nil { log.Fatalf("failed to create pipeline: %v", err) } log.Printf("created pipeline: %s (state: %s)", pipeline.ID, pipeline.State) }}}

    The pipeline starts in draft state. Activate it once you're ready to start processing events.

    Next steps

    Now that events are flowing, read Handling errors & retries to see what happens when a write fails, or Monitoring & alerts to watch it run.

    {{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/60d7d27a-ceda-4034-b98e-8b1181ca5c84}}|prev_label=Guides|next_href={{cms:item/3448ffab-598c-46e7-bda6-e7cdc4a1e7c6}}|next_label=Connecting a data source}}

Transforming events in flight

{{ds:component/docs-toc|items_html=
  • Reshaping events
  • Filtering events
  • Enriching with external data
  • Chaining transforms
  • Monitoring transform failures
    • }}

    Once events enter your pipeline, you can reshape them, filter out unwanted records, or add enrichment data from external sources — all before they reach their destination.

    Reshaping events

    Use a transform to extract, rename, or restructure fields from incoming events. Transforms are JavaScript functions that receive an event and return a modified version of it.

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=transform.js|language=javascript|code=export default function transform(event) {\n return {\n user_id: event.customer_id,\n name: event.first_name + ' ' + event.last_name,\n email: event.contact_email,\n created_at: new Date(event.signup_timestamp).toISOString()\n };\n}}}

    Return null from a transform to drop an event entirely, or throw an error to send it to the dead-letter queue.

    Filtering events

    Add a filter condition to your transform to block unwanted records at the source. A filter that returns false discards the event; true passes it through.

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=filter.js|language=javascript|code=export default function filter(event) {\n // Only pass through events from paying customers\n return event.plan_type !== 'free';\n}}} {{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Filters are fast|body_html=

    Filtering in the pipeline is cheaper than transforming and sending to a destination, then filtering downstream. Apply filters early.

    }}

    Enriching with external data

    Your transform can call out to external APIs or databases to add data to each event. Be mindful of rate limits and latency — every enrichment call adds milliseconds to pipeline throughput.

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=enrich.js|language=javascript|code=export default async function enrich(event) {\n const response = await fetch(`https://api.example.com/users/${event.user_id}`);\n const userData = await response.json();\n \n return {\n ...event,\n user_tier: userData.tier,\n account_balance: userData.balance\n };\n}}} {{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Async transforms add latency|body_html=

    Each external call blocks the pipeline for that event. Use with caution on high-throughput pipelines or consider batching lookups with a scheduled task instead.

    }}

    Chaining transforms

    A single transform stage can run multiple functions in sequence. The output of one becomes the input to the next.

    Monitoring transform failures

    If a transform throws, the event is retried according to your retry policy. Watch transform error rates in Monitoring & alerts.

    {{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/3448ffab-598c-46e7-bda6-e7cdc4a1e7c6}}|prev_label=Connecting a data source|next_href={{cms:item/062cc815-2b65-45b1-b36c-6ea67dfd1a0c}}|next_label=Handling errors & retries}}

Error handling & recovery

{{ds:component/docs-toc|items_html=
  • Automatic retries
  • Dead-lettering
  • Replaying events
  • Watching for failures
    • }}

    Every event that fails a transform or a destination write is retried automatically. This guide covers how that works and what to do when retries run out.

    Automatic retries

    Failed events retry with exponential backoff — 1s, 2s, 4s, up to a per-pipeline configurable ceiling. Most transient failures (a destination hiccup, a rate-limited third party) resolve within the first few attempts.

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline-retry-config.json|language=json|code={\n \"retry_policy\": {\n \"max_attempts\": 5,\n \"backoff\": \"exponential\",\n \"initial_delay_ms\": 1000\n }\n}}}

    Dead-lettering

    An event that exhausts its retries is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped silently.

    {{ds:component/alert|variant=danger|title=Dead-lettered events don't retry themselves|body_html=

    Once in the dead-letter queue, an event stays there until you replay it or explicitly discard it — it will not retry again on its own.

    }}

    Replaying events

    Use the Events endpoint's replay action to re-run a specific dead-lettered event once the underlying issue is fixed.

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=replay.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/events/evt_8f2c1a90/replay \\\n -H \"Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY\"}}

    Watching for failures

    Subscribe to pipeline.failed via Webhooks so you find out about dead-lettered events before a customer does. See also Monitoring & alerts.

    {{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/00ae9a4e-7788-4e8e-906a-f65b23820ba2}}|prev_label=Transforming events in flight|next_href={{cms:item/dc9f1302-e173-4034-9581-d06efea7d090}}|next_label=Scheduling & triggers}}

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=replay.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/events/evt_8f2c1a90/replay \\\n -H \"Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY\"}}

    Watching for failures

    Subscribe to pipeline.failed via Webhooks so you find out about dead-lettered events before a customer does. See also Monitoring & alerts.
